analysis.one_liner: Exempts federal construction contracts under $250,000 from prevailing-wage rules and redefines the prevailing wage as local average pay.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: despite 110 cosponsors, it sat in a House subcommittee until the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: The Davis-Bacon Act, a 1931 law, requires federal construction contractors to pay the "prevailing wage" in the area, which has historically been set at union scale. This bill would have exempted federal contracts under $250,000 from that rule, redefined the prevailing wage as the wage most local private-sector workers actually earn, created a lower-paid "helper" job classification, and cut payroll reporting from weekly to quarterly. It would have cut contractors' labor costs and federal construction spending, while lowering the wage floor for construction workers on federal projects.
analysis.who_benefits: Nonunion and small construction contractors, who could bid on federal jobs without union-scale payroll obligations, less paperwork, and a lower, average-based wage standard. The bill's stated rationale also includes savings for federal taxpayers on construction costs. A small safeguard — direct payment of back wages to workers from withheld contract funds — would also help workers who are shorted.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the Davis-Bacon coverage threshold from $2,000 to $250,000, exempting nearly all federal construction contracts from prevailing-wage obligations and making it easier for small contractors to win federal work without union-scale payroll compliance.

Redefines the prevailing wage as the wage paid to a majority of local private-industry workers, or their weighted average, and excludes wages on federal projects from the calculation — replacing the union-scale determination with a lower, market-average standard.
Creates a separate semi-skilled 'helper' classification with its own prevailing wage, which the bill presents as a way to open job opportunities for less-skilled workers.
Reduces Copeland Act certified payroll reporting from weekly statements to statements at the start, midpoint, and end of a contract, at least every three months, cutting paperwork for contractors.

Keeps two protections: an anti-contract-splitting rule barring agencies and contractors from carving projects into pieces under $250,000 to dodge the wage rules, and direct payment of wages found due to workers from money withheld under the contract rather than routing them through the Comptroller General.

analysis.who_pays: Construction workers on federal projects, whose wage floor would drop as union-scale determinations are replaced by local average wages, federal-project wages are excluded from the calculation, and most contracts become exempt altogether. Union contractors and union apprenticeship systems would also face competition from lower-wage bids.

drawbacks.text: Raising the coverage threshold from $2,000 to $250,000 would remove the prevailing-wage floor from nearly all federal construction, cutting pay for laborers and mechanics on federal jobs.

Computing the prevailing wage as a weighted average of local private wages, with federal-project wages excluded, would lower the wage standard itself rather than just clarify it — the savings come substantially out of workers' paychecks.
The new semi-skilled 'helper' class could substitute lower-paid helpers for journeymen, diluting skilled-trade employment and apprenticeship on federal work.

Enforcement of the anti-contract-splitting rule is constrained: the Labor Secretary must notify an agency within 180 days after construction is completed that an investigation will occur, a short window for uncovering a split done to evade the wage rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated goals — cost savings on federal construction, less paperwork, and easier entry for small contractors — are real and the anti-splitting and direct back-wage provisions are genuine safeguards. But the mechanism for most of the savings is lowering or removing the wage floor: the threshold exemption, the average-based wage definition, the exclusion of federal-project wage data, and the helper classification all push down what construction workers on federal jobs would earn. Weighing contractor and taxpayer savings against reduced pay for a large blue-collar workforce, the costs fall more heavily on working people than the benefits do.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, referred to the House Education and Labor Committee, then to its Labor Standards subcommittee, and never came up for a vote before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Charlie Stenholm, a conservative Texas Democrat, introduced the bill on May 4, 1989 with more than 100 original cosponsors, most of them Republicans.
The bill went to the House Education and Labor Committee and, on June 9, 1989, was referred to its Subcommittee on Labor Standards, where no markup or vote was ever scheduled.
On July 25, 1989 the Department of Defense submitted executive comment on the bill, the only further action recorded.
No floor vote ever happened, and the bill died when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Union-scale construction workers and the unions that represent them kept existing prevailing-wage protections; nonunion contractors who sought the exemption and lower wage standards got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Union-scale construction workers and their unions

for.name: Charles W. Stenholm
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Davis-Bacon Reform Act of 1989 and recruited a large original cosponsor list.

for.name: 94 of 175 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, providing most of its 110 signers.

for.name: 16 of 257 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Crossed party lines to cosponsor the bill.

against.what_they_did: Received the bill, sent it to the Subcommittee on Labor Standards, and never scheduled a markup or a floor vote.

against.name: Building and construction trades unions
against.what_they_did: Have historically opposed changes that weaken Davis-Bacon prevailing-wage protections, which are set at union scale.

sides.party_line_note: Support leaned heavily Republican — 94 of 175 House Republicans cosponsored versus 16 of 257 House Democrats — though the sponsor was a Democrat.

industries.note: The $250,000 exemption, the average-based wage definition, the exclusion of federal-project wage data, and the lower-paid helper class would all cut these contractors' labor costs on federal work. Their gain comes primarily out of the wages of construction workers on those jobs.

Davis-Bacon wage floors protect union contractors from being underbid on federal work; an average-based standard and broad exemption would erode that protection. The anti-contract-splitting rule offers them only partial offset.

Davis-Bacon determinations have historically been set at union scale; redefining the prevailing wage as the local private-sector average and creating a semi-skilled helper class would directly reduce union members' wages and job classifications on federal projects.
